13: ## Abstract
14: 
15: Drag on smooth circular cylinders is a canonical problem in fluid mechanics and a standard validation case for experiments and simulations. We report tow-tank measurements for three smooth cylinders with diameters of 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm, all with a wetted length of 0.60 m, towed at ten speeds between 0.2 and 1.1 m/s. The 30 runs span Reynolds numbers \(Re = UD/\nu\) from \(4.7\times10^{3}\) to \(5.0\times10^{4}\), with the water temperature measured for every run and used to evaluate the viscosity. Drag is obtained from a calibrated load cell, with the mean taken over a 5 s steady window. After rejecting one run affected by a post-run zero offset of 82 mV (3.85 N), the remaining 29 runs give a mean drag coefficient \(C_D = 1.151 \pm 0.030\) (2.6% run-to-run scatter). The three diameter means agree to within 1.5%, and no consistent Reynolds-number dependence is resolved across the three diameters. The streamwise force fluctuations are quasi-periodic and scale with tow speed and cylinder diameter. Interpreting the dominant drag fluctuation as twice the vortex-shedding frequency gives a Strouhal number \(St = 0.201 \pm 0.003\), independent of diameter and Reynolds number. The results are consistent with the subcritical regime of a smooth circular cylinder and provide a documented benchmark dataset, including the raw records, processing code and uncertainty discussion. Solid blockage is estimated at 2.3–4.5% and is not corrected; this is the main systematic limitation of the dataset.
16: 
17: **Keywords:** circular cylinder · drag coefficient · tow tank · Reynolds number · Strouhal number · load-cell calibration
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1 Introduction
22: 
23: The flow past a circular cylinder is one of the most studied configurations in fluid mechanics. Its drag coefficient \(C_D\) and vortex-shedding frequency, usually expressed as the Strouhal number \(St = f_s D/U\), are central to the design of offshore structures, moorings, cables, risers, masts and sensors, and they are widely used to validate computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and experimental facilities. The canonical behaviour is conveniently divided into Reynolds-number regimes (Roshko 1961; Zdravkovich 1997; Schlichting and Gersten 2017). In the subcritical regime, roughly \(10^{3} \lesssim Re \lesssim 2\times10^{5}\), the boundary layers remain laminar, separation occurs before the apex at roughly \(80^{\circ}\) from the front stagnation point, and the drag coefficient is approximately constant at \(C_D \approx 1.1\)–1.2. The Strouhal number is approximately 0.2. At higher Reynolds numbers the boundary layers become turbulent, the separation point moves downstream, and the drag coefficient falls through the critical regime before rising again in the transcritical regime (Achenbach 1968; Roshko 1961).
24: 
25: Even within the subcritical regime, measured drag coefficients are sensitive to surface roughness, free-stream turbulence, aspect ratio, end conditions and blockage. Reported values therefore scatter by several percent, and facility-specific benchmarks remain useful. Tow tanks are attractive for such measurements because the model is moved through quiescent water at a controlled speed, the free-stream turbulence is low, and the relative velocity is well defined. The same configuration also introduces practical difficulties: the drag force at low speed can be small compared with the load-cell resolution, the zero can drift during a run, and the finite tank width and depth produce blockage and free-surface effects.
26: 
27: This paper documents a tow-tank dataset for three smooth circular cylinders of different diameters, tested over overlapping Reynolds-number ranges with the same wetted length and the same nominal speeds. The specific objectives are to:
28: 
29: 1. measure the mean drag coefficient over \(Re \approx 4.7\times10^{3}\)–\(5.0\times10^{4}\) using per-run water-temperature corrections;
30: 2. test whether the drag coefficient depends on cylinder diameter at matched Reynolds number;
31: 3. extract the vortex-shedding frequency from the streamwise force signal and compare the resulting Strouhal number with the established value \(St \approx 0.2\); and
32: 4. document the calibration, repeatability, zero-drift rejection and blockage limitations of the dataset.
33: 
34: The contribution is deliberately a careful, open benchmark rather than a claim of new flow physics. The processed data, the run log and the analysis scripts accompany the paper.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2 Experimental methods
39: 
40: ### 2.1 Facility and models
41: 
42: The experiments were performed in a tow tank with a rectangular cross-section \(0.90\) m wide and \(0.75\) m deep. The tank length and the water depth during the tests are [to be completed]. Three smooth circular cylinders with nominal diameters \(D = 25.4\) mm (1 in), \(38.1\) mm (1.5 in) and \(50.8\) mm (2 in) were tested. Each cylinder had a wetted length \(L = 0.60\) m, giving aspect ratios \(L/D = 23.6\), \(15.7\) and \(11.8\), respectively. The cylinder material, surface finish and mounting arrangement are [to be completed].
43: 
44: The water temperature was recorded for each run and varied between \(13.7\) and \(17.6\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) across the three campaigns. The tow speed was varied from 0.2 to 1.1 m/s in increments of 0.1 m/s. Ten speeds were run for each diameter, giving 30 runs in total (Table 1). The three campaigns were performed on 14 October 2025 (25.4 mm), 3 November 2025 (50.8 mm) and 12 March 2026 (38.1 mm). The corresponding Reynolds-number ranges overlap substantially, which allows the diameter dependence to be examined at approximately matched \(Re\).
45:

54: ### 2.2 Force measurement and calibration
55: 
56: The drag force was measured with a load cell mounted [in line with the cylinder; model and range to be completed]. The load cell was calibrated with known masses in September 2025, before the October and November campaigns, and again in March 2026 after it had been remounted. Linear fits of voltage against weight gave sensitivities of \(0.020006\) V/N and \(0.021292\) V/N, respectively. The maximum calibration residual was below \(0.36\) mV, equivalent to about \(0.02\) N. The 6.4% change in sensitivity after remounting is larger than the calibration residual and shows why the cell must be recalibrated after any mechanical change.
57: 
58: Data were acquired at 200 Hz for 12 s per run. The September and November campaigns used the original DAQ format with a comma-separated time–voltage file; the March campaign used updated software with a semicolon-separated format. The raw records were processed with the scripts described in the data-availability statement.
59: 
60: ### 2.3 Data reduction
61: 
62: For each run, the load-cell zero was taken as the mean voltage during the first second, before the carriage accelerated. The drag force was then
63: 
64: \[
65: F(t) = \frac{V(t) - V_{\mathrm{tare}}}{S},
66: \]
67: 
68: where \(S\) is the calibration sensitivity. The steady window was defined as \(3 < t < 8\) s, which excludes the acceleration and deceleration transients (Fig. 1). The run mean \(\bar{F}\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_F\) were computed over this window.
69: 
70: The drag coefficient was evaluated from
71: 
72: \[
73: C_D = \frac{\bar{F}}{\frac{1}{2}\rho U^{2} D L},
74: \]
75: 
76: where \(\rho\) is the water density at the measured temperature and \(L = 0.60\) m is the wetted length. The Reynolds number was evaluated from
77: 
78: \[
79: Re = \frac{UD}{\nu(T)},
80: \]
81: 
82: with the kinematic viscosity obtained from a Vogel-type correlation for water at the measured temperature. Using the actual temperature rather than a fixed 20 °C changes \(Re\) by up to about 17% for the coldest runs; even between the coldest and warmest runs the difference is about 10%. This is important when comparing the three campaigns. The density was evaluated with the Kell correlation; its temperature dependence is weak and changes \(C_D\) by less than 0.3% over the present range.
83: 
84: ### 2.4 Quality control and uncertainty
85: 
86: The load-cell zero was checked before and after every run by comparing the mean voltage for \(t<1\) s with the mean for \(t>10.5\) s. For 29 of the 30 runs the difference was below \(0.06\) mV, equivalent to \(0.003\) N. Run 17 (50.8 mm cylinder, 0.8 m/s) showed an offset of \(82\) mV, equivalent to \(3.85\) N, and was rejected; the details are given in Section 3.4.
87: 
88: The empirical run-to-run scatter in \(C_D\) is \(0.030\), or 2.6% of the mean. This is the dominant contribution for most runs, although at the lowest speed the calibration residual of about \(0.02\) N is a significant fraction of the 0.33 N force. We use the run-to-run scatter as the repeatability estimate. It includes genuine unsteady-loading variability, small speed and temperature differences, and residual mounting effects. The largest systematic uncertainty is the blockage of the finite tank, estimated below; the wetted length and the cylinder diameter tolerance also contribute but were not independently measured in this dataset. [A full uncertainty budget with instrument accuracies should be added before submission.]
89: 
90: Solid blockage was estimated from the frontal-area ratio
91: 
92: \[
93: \frac{D L}{W H},
94: \]
95: 
96: where \(W = 0.90\) m and \(H = 0.75\) m are the tank width and depth. This assumes that the water depth equals the tank depth; if the water surface was lower, the blockage estimates increase. It gives 2.3%, 3.4% and 4.5% for the 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm cylinders, respectively. No blockage correction was applied. A Maskell-type correction (Maskell 1963) would require pressure or wake measurements that were not made, and the correction is therefore left as a limitation rather than applied speculatively.

100: ## 3 Results
101: 
102: ### 3.1 Force traces
103: 
104: Figure 1 shows a representative record (run 5, 25.4 mm cylinder, \(U = 0.6\) m/s). The carriage accelerates from rest between about 1.5 and 2.5 s, the force reaches a plateau by 3 s, and the steady window ends at 8 s before deceleration. The mean force in the window is 3.10 N with a standard deviation of 0.14 N, or 4.6% of the mean. The fluctuation is quasi-periodic rather than random, which is consistent with vortex shedding. Across all valid runs the coefficient of variation of the force is \(4.8\% \pm 0.5\%\), with no clear dependence on diameter.
105: 
106: ![Figure 1](figures/fig1_force_trace.png)
107: 
108: **Figure 1.** Representative drag-force record (run 5: 25.4 mm cylinder, \(U = 0.6\) m/s). The shaded region is the steady window \(3 < t < 8\) s used for the mean and standard deviation. The load-cell zero is stable to better than 0.1 mV over the record.
109: 
110: ### 3.2 Drag coefficient versus Reynolds number
111: 
112: Figure 2 shows \(C_D\) against \(Re\) for all valid runs, and Table 2 summarises the results by cylinder. The overall mean is
113: 
114: \[
115: C_D = 1.151 \pm 0.030 \qquad (n = 29),
116: \]
117: 
118: where the uncertainty is one standard deviation of the run-to-run values. Individual values range from 1.093 to 1.216. The three diameter means are 1.143, 1.152 and 1.157 for the 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm cylinders, respectively. The largest difference is 1.2%, which is well within the 2.6% run-to-run scatter; a one-way analysis of variance gives \(F(2,26) = 0.50\), far below the 5% critical value. We therefore resolve no significant diameter dependence at the present precision.
119: 
120: The data show only a weak and inconsistent Reynolds-number trend. A least-squares fit of \(C_D\) against \(\log_{10} Re\) for all valid runs gives a slope of \(+0.058\) per decade, corresponding to a change of about 0.06 over the full range. The per-cylinder slopes are \(+0.107\) (25.4 mm), \(+0.072\) (38.1 mm) and \(-0.006\) (50.8 mm). The 25.4 mm cylinder shows the most visible increase, from 1.093 at \(Re = 4.7\times10^{3}\) to 1.181 at \(Re = 2.6\times10^{4}\), but the two lowest-Reynolds points of that series are also the two lowest \(C_D\) values in the dataset. At the lowest speed the measured force is only 0.33 N, so part of this trend may reflect force resolution and residual zero drift rather than a physical Reynolds-number effect.
121: 
122: The highest valid \(C_D\) is 1.216 for the 50.8 mm cylinder at \(Re = 4.5\times10^{4}\). The next run in that series, at \(Re = 5.0\times10^{4}\), returns to 1.129. This non-monotonic behaviour is consistent with unsteady loading and measurement scatter; it does not support a systematic Reynolds-number trend over the present range.
123:

125: 
126: **Figure 2.** Drag coefficient versus Reynolds number for the three cylinders. Open symbols are individual runs; the dashed line is the overall mean \(C_D = 1.151\) and the shaded band is \(\pm 1\) standard deviation (0.030). Run 17 is omitted because of the zero drift discussed in Section 3.4. Reynolds numbers use the per-run water temperature.

137: ### 3.3 Vortex shedding from the streamwise force
138: 
139: The streamwise force on a circular cylinder fluctuates predominantly at twice the vortex-shedding frequency, because vortices are shed alternately from the two sides of the wake. We therefore identified the dominant frequency \(f_{\mathrm{drag}}\) of the steady-window force signal by a Hann-windowed Fourier transform and defined the shedding frequency as \(f_s = f_{\mathrm{drag}}/2\). The corresponding Strouhal number is \(St = f_s D/U = f_{\mathrm{drag}} D/(2U)\).
140: 
141: The dominant drag frequency increases linearly with \(U/D\), from 1.6 Hz for the 50.8 mm cylinder at 0.2 m/s to 17.4 Hz for the 25.4 mm cylinder at 1.1 m/s. The resulting Strouhal numbers collapse onto a single value (Fig. 3):
142: 
143: \[
144: St = 0.201 \pm 0.003 \qquad (n = 29),
145: \]
146: 
147: with individual values between 0.197 and 0.209. The per-cylinder means are 0.201, 0.202 and 0.201, and there is no visible trend with \(Re\) or \(D\). The 5 s window contains at least four shedding cycles at the lowest speed and more than 40 at the highest, so the peak is resolved for all runs. The bin spacing of the 5 s window is 0.2 Hz in drag frequency; the observed run-to-run scatter in \(St\) is 0.003, and the smooth scaling in Fig. 3 indicates that the peak location is better resolved than the raw bin width.
148: 
149: The agreement with the classical subcritical value \(St \approx 0.2\) supports the force records and indicates that the load cell is resolving the unsteady wake loading rather than facility vibration. It also provides an independent check on the tow speed: a systematic speed error would shift \(St\) away from 0.2.
150: 
151: ![Figure 3](figures/fig3_strouhal.png)
152: 
153: **Figure 3.** Strouhal number versus Reynolds number, obtained from the dominant streamwise force frequency as \(St = f_{\mathrm{drag}}D/(2U)\). The dashed line is the overall mean \(St = 0.201\) and the shaded band is \(\pm 1\) standard deviation (0.003).
154: 
155: ### 3.4 Rejected run
156: 
157: Run 17 (50.8 mm cylinder, \(U = 0.8\) m/s) was excluded from the primary analysis. Its post-run zero was 82 mV higher than its pre-run zero, equivalent to 3.85 N or 29% of the measured mean force. The uncorrected \(C_D\) is 1.355, about 18% above the overall mean, and its force standard deviation is also elevated. A simple linear interpolation of the zero between the pre- and post-run values reduces the mean force to about 11.4 N and gives \(C_D \approx 1.17\), consistent with the neighbouring runs. Because the drift mechanism is not known, we prefer to reject the run rather than apply an ad hoc correction. The raw record is retained in the dataset so that the rejection can be reproduced.
158:

160: 
161: ## 4 Discussion
162: 
163: ### 4.1 Comparison with established values
164: 
165: The mean drag coefficient \(C_D = 1.151\) lies within the range commonly reported for smooth circular cylinders in the subcritical regime, \(C_D \approx 1.1\)–1.2 (Tritton 1959; Wieselsberger 1921; Schlichting and Gersten 2017). The Strouhal number \(St = 0.201\) is likewise consistent with the classical value of about 0.2 (Roshko 1961; Norberg 2003). The fact that two independent quantities—the mean drag and the unsteady shedding frequency—agree with established values increases confidence in the calibration and data reduction.
166: 
167: The weak positive Reynolds-number trend seen for the 25.4 mm cylinder is opposite to the slight decrease often reported over the subcritical range. We do not interpret it as a physical effect for three reasons. First, the trend is not reproduced by the 50.8 mm cylinder, which covers a higher and wider \(Re\) range. Second, the lowest-Reynolds points of the 25.4 mm series have the smallest forces (0.33 N at 0.2 m/s), where calibration residual and tare drift are relatively largest. Third, the run-to-run scatter is comparable to the total change across the series. A larger number of repeats at low speed, or a lower-range load cell, would be needed to resolve whether the trend is real.
168: 
169: ### 4.2 Blockage, aspect ratio and finite-length effects
170: 
171: The estimated solid blockage rises from 2.3% for the 25.4 mm cylinder to 4.5% for the 50.8 mm cylinder. In a closed tank, blockage accelerates the flow around the model and generally increases the measured drag; a Maskell-type correction would therefore reduce the reported \(C_D\), with the largest effect on the 50.8 mm case. We did not apply such a correction because the required pressure or wake data were not measured. The absence of a clear increase in \(C_D\) with diameter suggests that the blockage bias is not larger than the 2.6% scatter, but blockage and aspect ratio are partly confounded: the 50.8 mm cylinder also has the lowest \(L/D\) (11.8), which could reduce drag through end effects and partially offset the blockage increase. Separating these effects would require a larger tank, a longer cylinder, or a systematic variation of \(L/D\) at fixed \(D\).
172: 
173: The free-surface and end conditions are also [to be completed: describe whether the cylinder is vertical/horizontal, how it is mounted, and whether end plates or a false floor are used]. These details matter for comparing absolute \(C_D\) values with other facilities.
174: 
175: ### 4.3 Implications for the dataset
176: 
177: The dataset is most useful as a benchmark for the subcritical regime at moderate Reynolds numbers, and as a worked example of the practical issues in tow-tank force measurement: calibration changes after remounting, zero drift during a run, low-force resolution at the slowest speeds, and blockage in a finite tank. The processed forces, per-run temperatures and rejection flag are provided so that other groups can re-analyse the data with a different blockage correction or viscosity correlation.
178: 
179: The main limitations are the single facility, the absence of direct wake or pressure measurements, the limited Reynolds-number range, and the lack of an independent turbulence or velocity calibration. Future work should add repeat runs at the lowest speeds, a two-component force balance to measure lift and drag simultaneously, particle-image velocimetry or hot-film wake measurements, and a systematic blockage study using different cylinder diameters at matched \(L/D\).
180: 
181: ---
182: 
183: ## 5 Conclusions
184: 
185: We have reported tow-tank measurements of drag and vortex shedding for three smooth circular cylinders with diameters of 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm and a wetted length of 0.60 m. The 29 valid runs span \(Re = 4.7\times10^{3}\)–\(5.0\times10^{4}\), with per-run water-temperature corrections. The main results are:
186: 
187: 1. The mean drag coefficient is \(C_D = 1.151 \pm 0.030\), with no significant dependence on cylinder diameter over the present range.
188: 2. The drag coefficient is approximately Reynolds-number independent over the tested range; the weak positive trend for the smallest cylinder is comparable to the run-to-run scatter and is not reproduced at larger diameters.
189: 3. The streamwise force fluctuates quasi-periodically, and the dominant frequency scales with \(U/D\). Interpreting it as twice the shedding frequency gives \(St = 0.201 \pm 0.003\), independent of diameter and Reynolds number.
190: 4. One run was rejected because of an 82 mV post-run zero offset; the raw record and rejection criterion are documented.
191: 5. Solid blockage is estimated at 2.3–4.5% and is the main systematic limitation; no blockage correction was applied.
192: 
193: The results are consistent with established subcritical cylinder behaviour and provide a documented benchmark dataset for CFD validation and facility comparison.

17: ## Key analysis decisions
18: 
19: 1. **Water temperature is used per run.** The notebook used a fixed \(\nu = 1.004\times10^{-6}\) m²/s (20 °C). The run log has temperatures from 13.7 to 17.6 °C, so the draft uses the Vogel equation for dynamic viscosity and the Kell correlation for density, giving \(\nu(T)\). This changes \(Re\) by up to about 17% relative to a fixed 20 °C for the coldest runs (about 10% between the coldest and warmest runs). The effect on \(C_D\) itself is small (density only), but it matters when the three diameter series are compared at matched \(Re\).
20: 
21: 2. **Run 17 is rejected.** Run 17 (50.8 mm, 0.8 m/s) has a post-run zero 82 mV above its pre-run zero. At the March sensitivity of 0.021292 V/N that is 3.85 N, or 29% of the measured mean force. The uncorrected \(C_D\) is 1.355. A linear interpolation of the zero between the pre- and post-run values gives \(C_D \approx 1.17\), consistent with neighbouring runs. The draft rejects the run rather than applying an ad hoc correction. The raw record is kept and the rejection is documented.
22: 
23: 3. **The wetted length is \(L = 0.60\) m.** This resolves the old October discrepancy. `figures/cd_vs_re_oct.png` gives \(C_D \approx 0.94\)–1.01, which is a constant factor 0.857 below the current values. That factor is exactly \(0.60/0.70\): the old figure used \(L = 0.70\) m (and a fixed 20 °C viscosity). With \(L = 0.60\) m the values rise to about 1.09–1.18, consistent with the subcritical cylinder literature. The note “Cd ~0.98, bit low? check L (0.6 m submerged)” is therefore explained: the old plot used the wrong length.
24: 
25: 4. **Strouhal number is inferred from the drag fluctuation.** The load cell measures the streamwise force, which for a circular cylinder fluctuates predominantly at twice the vortex-shedding frequency. The draft defines \(f_s = f_{\mathrm{drag}}/2\) and \(St = f_s D/U\). The resulting \(St = 0.201 \pm 0.003\) is a strong independent check on the data. If you prefer not to make this inference, Fig. 3 and the associated text can be removed or reframed as a force-fluctuation frequency rather than a Strouhal number.
26: 
27: 5. **Blockage is estimated, not corrected.** The frontal-area ratio \(DL/(WH)\) with \(W = 0.90\) m and \(H = 0.75\) m gives 2.3%, 3.4% and 4.5% for the three diameters. This assumes the water depth equals the tank depth; if the water surface was lower, the blockage is larger. No Maskell correction is applied because the required pressure/wake data are not available. The draft treats this as the main systematic limitation.
28: 
29: 6. **The 2025 and 2026 calibrations are kept separate.** The September 2025 sensitivity is 0.020006 V/N; the March 2026 sensitivity is 0.021292 V/N after the load cell was remounted. The 6.4% change is larger than the calibration residual and is a useful methodological point in the paper. `process_b3.py` hard-codes 0.0213 V/N, which is consistent with the fit to four significant figures.

 ## Abstract
 
-Drag on smooth circular cylinders is a canonical problem in fluid mechanics and a standard validation case for experiments and simulations. We report tow-tank measurements for three smooth cylinders with diameters of 25.4, 38.1 and 50.8 mm, all with a wetted length of 0.60 m, towed at ten speeds between 0.2 and 1.1 m/s. The three diameter means agree to within 1.5%, and no consistent Reynolds-number dependence is resolved across the three diameters. The streamwise force fluctuations are quasi-periodic and scale with tow speed and cylinder diameter. Interpreting the dominant drag fluctuation as twice the vortex-shedding frequency gives a Strouhal number \(St = 0.201 \pm 0.003\), independent of diameter and Reynolds number. The results are consistent with the subcritical regime of a smooth circular cylinder and provide a documented benchmark dataset, including the raw records, processing code and uncertainty discussion. Solid blockage is estimated at 2.3–4.5% and is not corrected; this is the main systematic limitation of the dataset.
